clue.text: It does not come from boot- or even shoe-trees

definitions.text: It does not come from boot- or even shoe-trees

parts.words: It does not come from boot- or even shoe-trees
parts.note: a fragrant timber whose name looks as if it should grow on a tree that bears footwear, but the tree has nothing to do with sandals

explanation.surface: A remark about the wooden trees used to keep boots and shoes in shape.
explanation.walkthrough: Boot-trees and shoe-trees are shaped wooden forms put into footwear; the clue plays on the idea that a wood named after a sandal should come from such a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: This scented timber comes from an Asian tree of the genus Santalum, used in carving and perfume.

clue.text: One has it to kneel on or wear

indicators.note: it stands for the answer: has followed by it makes something to kneel on, so has is taken away

parts.note: a hassock is a cushion for kneeling on in church
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps a cushion for kneeling, or perhaps to wear.
explanation.walkthrough: One has it: HAS plus the answer gives HASSOCK, a church kneeling cushion; remove HAS to leave the garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A short stocking for the foot is an item of clothing that people put on.

clue.text: Turn one perhaps for the physicist

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of turn one might be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A physics lecturer might be asked to take a turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges TURN ONE into the uncharged particle studied by physicists.
explanation.definitionFit: This uncharged particle in the atomic nucleus is a central object of study in physics.

clue.text: A regular poser, no doubt

parts.note: a poser is someone who poses, and one who poses regularly for painters, rather than a puzzling question

explanation.surface: Someone describing a habitual puzzle or a show-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poser' suggests a tricky question or a show-off; here it is one who sits for painters as a job.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who sits still for painters or sculptors as a profession poses regularly.

clue.text: Surely not where the employees held their dance?

definitions.text: Surely not where the employees held their dance?

parts.words: Surely not where the employees held their dance?
parts.note: the ..., a dance for the staff of a factory, suggests a place where people work at a bench

explanation.surface: Doubting whether the staff party was really held at the factory.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'hop' is an informal dance and the 'works' is a factory's staff; split the word and it is the staff dance, but it really names a room for making things.
explanation.definitionFit: A room or building where things are made or repaired by hand or machine.

clue.text: One can get used to being put out

indicators.note: the question of what one can get from the words used to says their letters are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A person adjusting to being thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get used to' reads as becoming accustomed; 'One can get' rearranges USED TO into the word for put out.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone expelled or driven from a position has been removed by force.

clue.text: One in a stunning suit ?

parts.note: a card of one of the four suits, and also a cudgel, which stuns whoever it hits

explanation.surface: Someone wearing a dazzling outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stunning suit' reads as a dazzling outfit; it is the card suit whose emblem is a cudgel that stuns.
explanation.definitionFit: Any card of the black trefoil suit is one of these, and the same word names a heavy stick for striking.

clue.text: Her tale is garbled, but materially correct

indicators.note: a garbled tale is muddled, so the letters of her tale are mixed up

explanation.surface: A woman's story is muddled, though its facts are right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is garbled' rearranges HER TALE; 'materially correct' says the result is a material, as the hide is.
explanation.definitionFit: Tanned animal hide is a material, so a garble giving this word gets the material right.

clue.text: A creditor might be one in the advertising business

definitions.text: A creditor might be one in the advertising business

parts.words: A creditor might be one in the advertising business
parts.note: a creditor posts an invoice to a debtor, while the trade sense is a person who pastes up posters

explanation.surface: A lender who might also work in advertising.
explanation.walkthrough: A creditor posts a bill to the debtor; the same words name a man who pastes up advertising posters.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who sticks up placards and advertising notices on walls and hoardings.

clue.text: But unsuitable wear for tennis

parts.note: formal clothes for a royal court, not for a tennis court

explanation.surface: A warning about what not to wear on the tennis court.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennis is played on a court, so the solver is led to sportswear; the court meant is a royal one, with its ceremonial costume.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal ceremonial costume worn when presented at a royal palace, hardly fit for playing a sport.

clue.text: Catch Kruger, say ?

indicators.note: say signals that the name of Kruger is to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: Paul Kruger was the Boer president of the Transvaal

explanation.surface: Someone asking us to grab hold of a famous South African statesman.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Kruger led the Transvaal republic in the 1890s; his first name, said out loud, gives the engineering catch.
explanation.definitionFit: A pivoted bar that engages a ratchet wheel to stop it running back is a mechanical catch.

clue.text: Knee-breeches-—for Lilliputians?

definitions.meaning: breeches fastened at the knee, worn by men in the eighteenth century
the tiny people of Gulliver's Travels would wear tiny garments

explanation.surface: A tailor's note about knee-length trousers for tiny folk.
explanation.walkthrough: Lilliputians are the tiny people in Swift's Gulliver's Travels.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for close-fitting breeches, and taken literally, little garments fit for Swift's tiny people.

clue.text: Faculty he needs for the football team

indicators.note: HE is what this word still needs to become the team, so the team's name with he removed is what is left

parts.note: Heart of Midlothian, known as Hearts, is an Edinburgh football club
taken as written

explanation.surface: A university department asking what a man needs to join the football side.
explanation.walkthrough: Hearts is the Scottish football club Heart of Midlothian; put HE in front of the answer and the team appears.
explanation.definitionFit: A university division of humanities subjects is called a faculty, as in the Faculty of the humanities.

clue.text: The sides of the vessel are inside it

definitions.text: The sides of the vessel are inside it

indicators.note: the teams are placed within the word for the vessel, splitting it after its first letter

parts.note: a ship is a vessel
sides in sport are teams

explanation.surface: A remark that the hull's sides are contained within a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sides of the vessel' suggests a hull; the sides are teams, set inside SHIP after its S.
explanation.definitionFit: A powered sea-going craft is a vessel, and teams of passengers could travel inside one.

clue.text: Lucy Ashton and Catharine Glover, we hear, for instance

definitions.text: Lucy Ashton and Catharine Glover, we hear, for instance

indicators.note: we hear asks for the phrase that names these two to be said out loud

parts.note: heroines of Sir Walter Scott's novels The Bride of Lammermoor and The Fair Maid of Perth, so women of Scott

explanation.surface: A list naming two women as examples of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Both are Walter Scott's heroines, Scott's women; said out loud that is the word for women of Scotland, which both are.
explanation.definitionFit: Women from Scotland, as both these heroines are, Lucy from the Borders and Catharine from Perth.

clue.text: What can you get from this, old man? Not coins

indicators.text: What can you get from this
indicators.note: the question asks what can be made by rearranging letters, so the two words that follow are to be reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asking an elderly man what he can earn from something, adding that it won't be money.
explanation.walkthrough: The Old Man of Coniston is the fell above Coniston Water in England's Lake District, so 'old man' leads to the place. 'Not coins' rearranged gives it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lake District fell called the Old Man rises above this village and lake in Cumbria.

clue.text: Puffy booksellers

parts.note: short promotional puffs printed on book jackets, which help sell the books

explanation.surface: Shop assistants in a bookshop who are rather swollen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puffy' suggests swollen; a puff is publicity praise, and these pieces of praise sell books.
explanation.definitionFit: Promotional text on a book's jacket praises it to persuade readers to buy.

clue.text: Being "in the cart " is all in his day's work

definitions.text: Being "in the cart " is all in his day's work

parts.words: Being "in the cart " is all in his day's work
parts.note: to be in the cart is slang for being in trouble, but a man who drives a wagon is in his cart all day

explanation.surface: A man for whom being in trouble is routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the cart' is old slang for being in a fix; the driver of a horse-drawn wagon sits in his cart as a job.
explanation.definitionFit: A driver of a horse-drawn wagon spends his working day in his vehicle.

clue.text: Throw it back to the artist

indicators.note: back tells us the two words for throwing it are read from the end

parts.note: to throw is to toss
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to return an object to a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw it back' reads as returning something to a painter; 'back' is the reversal signal. James Tissot was a French painter who worked in London.
explanation.definitionFit: James Tissot was a nineteenth-century French painter of fashionable society scenes.

clue.text: Flora's bad marks ?

parts.note: Flora is plant life as well as a girl's name; marks of disgrace share their name with parts of a flower's pistil

explanation.surface: A girl called Flora has had poor results at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flora' looks like a girl's name, but means plants; the word for marks of shame also names the pollen-catching tips of flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Marks of disgrace, and also the parts of a flower's pistil that receive the pollen.

clue.text: Fathead in case of trouble has one hundred pounds in a bundle

parts.note: the head of the word fat is its first letter

indicators.note: the shuffled case holds the other pieces within it
the word case is in trouble, so its letters are disturbed

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling, from libra

explanation.surface: A stupid person in a crisis carries a hundred pounds in a parcel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fathead' looks like an insult but gives F. 'of trouble' rearranges the letters of 'case', and 'has' places one, hundred and pounds inside the jumble, just before its final E.
explanation.definitionFit: A fascicle is a small bunch, as of fibres or leaves, or an instalment of a book issued in parts.

clue.text: Where Sir John was left alone with his glory

definitions.text: Where Sir John was left alone with his glory

parts.words: Where Sir John was left alone with his glory
parts.note: the closing line of Charles Wolfe's poem on the burial of Sir John Moore, killed in battle in Spain

explanation.surface: Recalling the place where a knight was left to his fame.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Wolfe's poem on the burial of Sir John Moore ends 'We left him alone with his glory'; Moore died in battle at the Spanish port.
explanation.definitionFit: The Galician port, now A Coruna, where General Moore died in battle against the French in 1809.

clue.text: 5 to 4 on the winner? That's lively!

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral for five
IV is the Roman numeral for four
an ace is a winning card or a serve that wins the point

explanation.surface: Betting odds of five to four on the favourite make for excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: '5 to 4 on' reads as betting odds; the numbers are Roman numerals V and IV, joined to ACE.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical direction meaning brisk and spirited, from the Italian for lively.

clue.text: He needed two messengers, one to fetch and one to carry

definitions.text: He needed two messengers, one to fetch and one to carry

parts.words: He needed two messengers, one to fetch and one to carry
parts.note: the chess monarch in Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass, who keeps two messengers, one to come and one to go

explanation.surface: A busy man explaining why he employs a pair of couriers.
explanation.walkthrough: In Through the Looking-Glass the chess king has messengers Haigha and Hatta, and explains he must have two, one to fetch and one to carry.
explanation.definitionFit: A chess piece made a character by Lewis Carroll, whose Looking-Glass monarch keeps a pair of messengers.

clue.text: Eight in a row ?

parts.note: a rowing eight pulls eight blades together, so 'row' is the verb of rowing, not a line

explanation.surface: Eight things lined up one after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a row' reads as a line; it is the act of rowing, and an eight has eight blades.
explanation.definitionFit: Rowing eights carry eight crew, each pulling one of these long-bladed poles through the water.

clue.text: Now this will get you nowhere

indicators.note: now and this together get you nowhere, so this is what is left of nowhere once now is taken off

explanation.surface: A warning that some action is futile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this' stands for the answer: NOW plus it makes NOWHERE, so it is NOWHERE without NOW, a word meaning in this place.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb points to this place, the spot where the speaker is.

clue.text: Degrees of parenthood

parts.note: two Master of Arts degrees side by side spell a word for a parent

explanation.surface: Different levels of being a parent.
explanation.walkthrough: MA is the Master of Arts degree; two of them together give a child's word for mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Mother is called by this childish name, which is also two Master of Arts degrees written in a row.

clue.text: No doubt backers at cockfighting had an eye to it

definitions.text: No doubt backers at cockfighting had an eye to it

parts.words: No doubt backers at cockfighting had an eye to it
parts.note: a match of fighting cocks was called a main, so gamblers watched the chances in it, as self-seekers watch for profit

explanation.surface: Gamblers at a cockfight kept a look-out for something.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'main' was a cockfighting match; 'an eye to the main chance' means looking out for one's own profit.
explanation.definitionFit: To have an eye to this is to watch for personal advantage or the best opportunity for gain.

clue.text: Get home in fine style

indicators.note: in shows the answer is sitting inside the words fine style

explanation.surface: Arriving back at your house with some panache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get home in fine style' reads as arriving grandly; the bird's home sits inside 'fine style'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird's nest is its home, built for laying eggs and raising young.

clue.text: 12's team apparently relax in the garden!

parts.note: the answer to 12 across is what HE needs for a football team, Heart of Midlothian, the Edinburgh club
to relax is to ease

explanation.surface: A football squad seems to unwind among the flower beds.
explanation.walkthrough: Hearts, the Edinburgh club Heart of Midlothian, comes from 12 across (HE plus ARTS); add EASE. 'apparently' links.
explanation.definitionFit: The wild pansy, a small flower grown in gardens, has long carried this old name.
